During the height of the trade war between Trump and China, with tariffs rising almost weekly, companies such as Logitech quickly raised the prices of products sold in the United States by significant margins.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, to date no company has been seen passing on refunds to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit has now been launched in an attempt to address the issue…

Trump's tariff saga

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China as if imagining that imposing massive tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to relocate production lines back to the United States.

Of course, this was never a realistic prospect. The US lacks the infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to manufacture consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump kept claiming that tariffs were paid by China, but the reality is that the costs were ultimately borne by American brands importing finished goods — and those extra expenses were passed on to consumers through price hikes. At the most chaotic point of the saga, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers should be entitled to refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose those tariffs unilaterally, and stated that amounts paid by US businesses must be refunded — a process that is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately passed on to consumers through price hikes, yet the affected companies have shown no sign whatsoever of refunding their customers to date.

The law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period when the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's view

The principle is quite clear: companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the companies. Morally speaking, they should pass that money back to the consumers who purchased their products during that period.

In practice, however, this is likely to be extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify every transaction through its vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers paid, and calculate what proportion of those prices was attributable to tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it's worth noting that class-action suits typically benefit the lawyers the most, while the average payout to consumers tends to be modest.
